claims.text: The initial refractory high-entropy alloy is solutionized and homogeneous, without secondary-phase precipitates.
A single-step controlled aging treatment can nucleate and grow fine, coherent B2 or similar ordered nanoprecipitates.
Careful selection of aging temperature and time can produce nanoprecipitates without significant coarsening.
The aging treatment will generate a uniform distribution of fine, coherent B2 or equivalent ordered nanoprecipitates within the grain matrix.
The nanoprecipitates will impede dislocation motion through an Orowan-type mechanism.
Impeded dislocation motion will increase the alloy's high-temperature strength.
Producing nanoprecipitates by aging will impose no significant density penalty.
Precipitate coherency will preserve a uniform stress field.
The uniform stress field associated with coherent precipitates will minimize adverse effects on room-temperature ductility.
The aged alloy will have higher high-temperature yield strength than the solutionized baseline.
The high-temperature strength improvement is expected under sustained tensile or creep loading at approximately 1000 degrees Celsius.
Room-temperature mechanical properties will remain largely unchanged after aging relative to the solutionized baseline.
Excessive precipitate coarsening or formation of deleterious phases could compromise room-temperature performance.
An unfavorable precipitate size, number density, or coherency could cause embrittlement or alter room-temperature properties.
Failure to improve high-temperature yield strength or creep resistance beyond experimental error relative to the solutionized control would falsify the hypothesis.
A significant degradation of room-temperature performance relative to the solutionized control would falsify the hypothesis.
